description: Snow Geeks is a Chicago-based team building astronaut health monitoring software for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our roster is already set, and this page is open solely for our existing teammates to officially join!
summary: Crew Health is an offline health monitoring app for astronauts on long missions, where a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way. It compares each astronaut’s vital signs with their own pre-flight baseline, colours an interactive 3D body by status, and catches slow drifts before they become emergencies. When a reading needs action, such as during a solar storm, it immediately shows a step-by-step checklist drawn from cited NASA and clinical sources. Fixed rules make every decision; a local AI model only explains them in plain language and reads spoken or typed descriptions in an emergency, with no internet needed. A daily check-in covers vitals, sleep, mood, vision, pain, exercise and fluids, and is sent to a flight surgeon over a link that simulates the real signal delay. On Earth, every report is archived in Microsoft Azure. The app uses real NASA data, including a solar particle event from DONKI and Curiosity’s radiation measurements, while crew readings are simulated.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Crew Health is an offline health monitoring app for astronauts on long missions. On the way to Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way, and the link can drop for days, so astronauts must assess their own health and act before a doctor can answer.

Before launch, each astronaut sets up a profile that becomes their personal baseline. The home screen shows an interactive 3D body: organs are coloured green, amber or red by status, and a halo around the body shows radiation exposure. Vitals tiles show temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, sleep, water intake and blood sugar, and a Mission card tracks the day's radiation dose and the mission total against NASA's 600 mSv career limit.

Fixed rules compare every reading with the astronaut's own baseline and with cited limits, and flag slow drifts of 8% or more before any limit is crossed. When action is needed, such as during a solar storm, the app immediately shows a step-by-step checklist and alerts Earth. A daily check-in of six short assessments (vitals, mind and sleep, vision, body and pain, exercise, food and water) produces a report for the flight surgeon. In an emergency, "I need help" alerts the crew and Earth at once, then asks injury-specific questions plus fixed danger signs and shows the right steps. Every message reaches a flight surgeon screen with the real signal delay, and each one is archived in Microsoft Azure on Earth.

BENEFITS

Works without an internet connection, including AI and speech recognition.

Gives the astronaut steps immediately instead of waiting up to 44 minutes for a reply.

Catches gradual changes, not only emergencies, by measuring each person against their own normal.

Hands-free use: speak instead of typing, and have checklists read aloud.

Doctors review only what needs them: all-normal daily reports receive an automatic all-clear.

INTENDED IMPACT

Supporting crew autonomy on Artemis missions, future Mars missions and long stays on lunar or Martian bases. The same offline design could serve people far from medical help on Earth, such as Antarctic research stations, ships at sea and remote clinics.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

Python (standard library only) for the server and rules; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the screens.

three.js for the 3D body, built from the MakeHuman base mesh (public domain).

Ollama running Meta's Llama 3.2 locally, to explain readings and read symptom descriptions.

whisper.cpp running OpenAI's Whisper model locally, for offline speech to text.

Microsoft Azure Blob Storage for the Earth-side medical archive, with store-and-forward uploads.

NASA DONKI for a real solar particle event (5 September 2026); Curiosity RAD measurements for radiation levels on Mars and in transit; NASA-STD-3001 for radiation limits.

Apple Health export import for a real personal baseline.

Hardware: a standard laptop. Crew sensor readings are simulated, so no special hardware is required.

AI coding assistants (mainly Claude) helped write code; the design, sources and testing were the team's.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The 3D body turns, zooms and responds to touch, and its heart beats at the astronaut's own heart rate.

The communication delay is part of the design: the astronaut acts first, and Earth's reply arrives later, as it would in reality.

The AI never decides. Rules with cited limits choose every alert and checklist; the AI only explains them and shows which protocol its answer came from.

Mood is never shown in red, to avoid adding pressure or encouraging under-reporting; the flight surgeon still sees the real status.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Safety: no AI-made medical decisions, and fixed danger-sign questions in every emergency.

Scientific honesty: published limits are cited (NASA, CDC, American Heart Association, American Diabetes Association); limits we chose ourselves are labelled as such, and simulated data is marked as simulated.

Reliability: the crew side never depends on the cloud.

Accessibility: status is never shown by colour alone, controls are large, and the app supports speech and read-aloud.

Privacy: no real astronaut records; personal data and access keys stay out of the public code.

An astronaut who is unwell: short checklists, few taps, and one alert at a time.
